blocks.text: Cover a small, predictable surface: tokens API, theming API, and component APIs (props/events/slots).

Expose three main entry points: a tokens API (for spacing/typography/layout), a theming API (ThemeProvider / theme class or data-attribute), and a set of accessible components with consistent props and events. From a consumer perspective it feels like: wrap your app in a theme provider, import Button/Input/Dialog, and optionally read tokens when you need custom layout or one-off pieces.

Contract checks:
- Public component entry points and package side effects are explicit.
- Theme selection changes semantic color values; dir controls writing direction separately.
- Component APIs use consistent props, events, and slots.
- Accessible names and relationships are required when native visible content does not provide them.
- Consumer fixtures verify bundle retention and lazy boundaries.

blocks.title: Core API surfaces
rows: "The theme API controls light/dark/high-contrast and direction (LTR/RTL). It typically wraps the app and sets CSS variables + dir so components and custom layout both respect the current theme."
"Each component has its own entry point to allow tree-shaking. There can also be a main barrel (@acme/ds), but deep imports are first-class for performance-sensitive apps."
"All components share consistent prop patterns: variant, size, tone, disabled, onPress/onChange, etc. This reduces cognitive load and makes adoption easier."
"Slots allow flexible composition (icons, descriptions, custom content) without breaking accessibility. The API makes common patterns easy but doesn’t block advanced usage."
"Tokens are available in a typed object for advanced layouts and one-off pieces. Most teams use components, but tokens are there when you need custom composition."

blocks.title: Component API rules
items: Use consistent event names (e.g. onPress or onClick, not both).
Expose size in a normalized way (size="sm" | "md" | "lg").
Keep focus/ARIA inside components so consumers don’t need to wire low-level accessibility manually.
Support asChild/component overrides (optional) for advanced routing or polymorphism, while keeping default semantics sane.
Make API forward-compatible by reserving room for future tokens/variants.

blocks.title: Accessibility hooks in the API
items: Components with no visible label (icon-only buttons) require an aria-label prop.
Dialog/Modal components handle focus trap, aria-modal, and role="dialog" internally.
Tabs expose TabList, Tab, and TabPanel in a way that encourages correct relationships (ids/aria-controls wired automatically).
Form controls forward id, name, aria-describedby so integration with forms and validation is straightforward.
Tooltips follow tooltip disclosure behavior and never contain required interactive actions; menus use the menu pattern with their own trigger and arrow-key navigation.
High-contrast and dark-mode differences are handled by tokens, not extra props per component.

blocks.title: How consumers typically use the API

steps.title: 1. Wrap app with ThemeProvider
steps.text: At the root, the app selects a color theme through CSS variables and independently sets dir on the relevant document or subtree. Nested direction changes remain possible for mixed-language content.

steps.title: 2. Import components on demand
steps.text: Feature teams import only needed components from deep entry points (@acme/ds/button, @acme/ds/dialog) to keep bundles lean and tree-shakable.

steps.title: 3. Pass semantic props
steps.text: Teams configure components using semantic props (variant, tone, size) instead of raw colors or spacing values, ensuring consistency and easy theming.

steps.title: 4. Use tokens for custom layouts
steps.text: For layouts or low-level elements, teams read from the tokens API to align spacing, typography, and colors with the system without creating custom hard-coded styles.

steps.title: 5. Evolve with versions
steps.text: When the library releases new versions, teams see deprecation notices in docs/TS types, and can migrate using clear guides without digging into internals.

items.label: API goal
items.helperText: Props and events encourage good a11y patterns.

blocks.title: Contract checkpoint
blocks.text: From a consumer’s point of view, a good design system API feels boring and predictable: wrap in a theme, import a Button, pass a few semantic props, and get an accessible, themed component. All the complexity (tokens, dark mode, RTL, a11y wiring, tree-shaking) stays behind that API line.

Each component exposes a framework-appropriate public API but shares cross-framework behavioral acceptance tests when multiple implementations exist. Tokens are CSS custom properties or generated platform outputs with documented fallback. Private DOM shape and internal class names are not public contracts unless explicitly documented.

steps.title: Specify interaction contract
steps.text: Write interaction and accessibility behavior before implementation details.

steps.title: Build token-backed primitive
steps.text: Compose primitives and semantic tokens with strict public exports.

steps.title: Validate consumer behavior
steps.text: Run keyboard, screen-reader, theme, RTL, high-contrast, and composition tests.

steps.title: Release compatible package
steps.text: Classify compatibility, publish migration notes, and observe canary consumers.
